catalog_quote: [Thesis 3.6, p.62] Yelmek does not use suprasegmental features to distinguish words on a lexical level. There is no evidence for lexical tone or contrastive stress. ... [3.6.1] Although syllables vary in prominence, there is no conclusive evidence for word-level stress in Yelmek and I thus assume there is none. Syllable prominence varies over different instances of the same word in different contexts. ... [p.66] Even more striking is the fact that the perceived stress shifts from the second syllable to the third syllable (which is consistent with the measurements). ... Note that this shift occurs widely in Yelmek, not just for this particular word. ... Though the data indicated that the earlier a syllable appears in a given word, the more intense it tends to be and the later it is placed in a word, the higher the pitch tends to be. audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: The classification no word stress rests on the best and essentially only modern description of this exact lect: Gregor's 2021 ANU PhD grammar (457 pp) plus her 2021 instrumental-phonetic LD&C chapter, both held as PDF+text, and the deciding quotation is verbatim at the stated printed pages in both (thesis pp.62, 66; LD&C p.23). The author's conclusion is explicitly provisional ('cannot be conclusively answered at this stage'; possible 'stress ghosting'), which the record's the primary-stress rule already discloses; the stated analysis in both works is absence of word-level stress with prominence tracking utterance intonation, so the code is faithful. Glottolog's hh bibliography offers nothing better (Drabbe 1950 Dutch sketch; Tethool 2012 MA on a different Yelmek variety). No double count: sibling key yelm1242 is coded 'undetermined' on the same source. Only fix worth making is cosmetic: thesis pdf-page locator s
